evaluation.positioning_hook: A Napa college janitor secretly stalking young women is hunted by detectives and the girls he’s terrorized, only to expose a buried high-school humiliation that turned victim into predator.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, immediate fear engine and a built-in audience for stalking/revenge thrillers, especially with the campus setting and the masked intruder imagery. The hard-R sexual threat and repeated assault material narrow the buyer pool, and the script’s exploitation-forward presentation will play more niche than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast: a peeping tom escalates from voyeurism to assault, and the investigation eventually reveals the predator is tied to the women’s shared past. The picture-in-the-bedroom motif and the repeated hair-cutting signature make the threat easy to explain in one breath.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ashley, Megan, and Rosales each have distinct energy, and Janice’s late reveal gives the antagonist a strong hidden identity. But the script is driven more by function than by deep interiority for most of the ensemble, so the characters are vivid in scene but not especially durable beyond the premise.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The hair-cutting signature, the Tom Cruise mask, and the final Janice reveal give the script a specific, nasty identity. Still, the underlying structure is a familiar stalker-thriller with a revenge-backstory reveal, and much of the execution leans on genre convention.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The attacks escalate cleanly, the police investigation keeps the pressure moving, and the Halloween sequence gives the story a strong late-game engine. There is some repetition in the attack pattern, but the reveal of Wesley, then the Janice twist, keeps the momentum alive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script has a fresh surface-level hook in the repeated mutilation of hair as a calling card and the eventual inversion of the obvious suspect. What keeps it from a higher score is that the emotional logic of the revenge backstory arrives late and the central mystery is more procedural than revelatory.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Napa college environment, the social dynamics among the girls, and the police work give the story a workable social world. But the world mostly functions as a container for stalking set pieces rather than a deeply generative system with layered institutions and rules.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct sleazy, mean, tabloid-thriller register, with crude banter colliding against genuine menace. The tonal identity is consistent and recognizable, even if it lives close to exploitation territory rather than a more elevated thriller lane.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The Samantha/Janice reveal and the old-photo flashbacks suggest a deeper wound under the stalking plot, and the girls’ shared history gives the story some buried emotional material. That said, the script keeps returning to the same threat pattern, so the depth is present but not fully mined.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The girls’ group dynamic is lively, argumentative, and easy to track, and the police team adds a second relationship engine. The script gets real mileage from the women’s banter and shared history, though the ensemble is still subordinate to the central predator-victim structure.

lead_characters.name: Megan McKnight
lead_characters.hook: Megan is the story’s emotional center: the most grounded of the core girls, the one who clocks danger early, tries to keep the group together, and carries the burden of being the responsible friend in a room full of chaos. She’s smart, wary, and increasingly trapped between disbelief, fear, and the need to protect the people around her.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a grounded thriller lead like Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs or Naomi Watts in Mulholland Drive: a role that lets an actor play intelligence, alarm, and moral pressure while staying emotionally readable under siege.

lead_characters.name: Ashley Sloan
lead_characters.hook: Ashley is the sharp-tongued wild card, the one who masks fear with provocation, sexual bravado, and a hard shell built around old trauma. Her anger at men is not just attitude; the script gives her a buried abuse history that makes her both comic relief and one of the story’s most wounded survivors.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the bite-and-vulnerability showcase of Christina Ricci in The Opposite of Sex or Jennifer Jason Leigh in Single White Female: fast, funny, abrasive, and then suddenly devastating.

lead_characters.name: Sarah Puckett
lead_characters.hook: Sarah is the group’s self-destructive pressure valve, drinking too much, flirting with disaster, and becoming the first major victim of the predator’s escalation. She’s written as reckless and funny on the surface, but the script uses her disappearance to turn the threat from creepy to catastrophic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong victim-to-catalyst material in the vein of a standout supporting turn in a horror-thriller like Drew Barrymore in Scream: a role that can be light, messy, and then abruptly become the emotional alarm bell.

lead_characters.name: Lauren Adams
lead_characters.hook: Lauren is the polished, protected one whose attack lands like a violation of the group’s sense of safety. She reads as the more conventional ‘nice girl’ in the ensemble, which makes her victimization feel especially invasive and public.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This gives an actor the clean, sympathetic vulnerability of a classic thriller supporting role — the kind that lets them play fear, humiliation, and aftermath in a contained but memorable arc.

lead_characters.name: Brittany Sheppard
lead_characters.hook: Brittany is the more socially observant member of the group, often functioning as the one who notices the weirdness and asks the question everyone else avoids. Her attack and aftermath deepen the sense that the predator is working through the friend group with methodical intent.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble-thriller role that lets an actor play alertness, fear, and aftermath without needing to carry the whole movie — a solid showcase for a rising character actor.

lead_characters.name: Heather Pennington
lead_characters.hook: Heather is quieter and more emotionally exposed than Ashley, and the script uses her family background to underline how much of the group’s pain is rooted in old neglect and old shame. Her attack and hospital scenes give the story one of its more vulnerable aftershocks.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a strong aftermath lane — the emotional fallout territory seen in supporting turns like Rachel True in The Craft, where the damage matters as much as the attack.

lead_characters.name: Janice Evans
lead_characters.hook: Janice is the polished, slightly smug professor who initially reads as a campus authority figure and later becomes the story’s most loaded reveal. The final twist reframes her as Samantha grown up, carrying a buried grievance that has been waiting for decades to surface.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal, dual-identity role that gives an actor a real transformation showcase — the performance territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects, where the audience’s understanding of the character flips.

lead_characters.name: Wesley Jarvis
lead_characters.hook: Wesley is the false lead: the harmless-looking janitor whose loneliness, resentment, and voyeurism make him a credible suspect and a real threat. He’s written as sexually predatory and socially pathetic, which makes him useful as a red herring and a mid-story escalation point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally ugly supporting role that character actors love — the showcase territory of a Dennis Franz or Michael Rooker type, where menace is built from ordinariness and self-justification.

lead_characters.name: Detective Rosales
lead_characters.hook: Rosales is the competent, no-nonsense investigator who keeps the story from floating away into pure sleaze. She’s practical, skeptical, and one of the few adults in the room who can match the girls’ urgency with actual authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded procedural authority role that gives an actor the crisp, controlled energy of Regina King in a crime drama — smart, direct, and able to carry exposition without flattening the scene.

lead_characters.name: Buck Blevins
lead_characters.hook: Buck is the rough-edged, instinctive detective who pushes the case forward through bluster, suspicion, and a willingness to get dirty. He’s the story’s most colorful law-enforcement voice, and the one most likely to say the thing everyone else is thinking.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing cop role that lets an actor do swagger, comic aggression, and dogged instinct in the vein of William H. Macy or Brian Dennehy in a crime picture.

lead_characters.name: Margo
lead_characters.hook: Margo is the social-climbing, emotionally armored mother whose old cruelty becomes the story’s buried moral wound. She’s the most openly defensive of the women from the past, and the one whose refusal to face guilt gives the backstory its sharpest edge.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige supporting territory for an actress who can play status, denial, and buried shame — the kind of role that gives someone the sharp, poisonous authority of Laura Linney in a family drama.

casting_characteristics: one major female antagonist reveal in her 40s
one child victim scene in the bar parking lot

notable_requirements: multiple suburban homes with accessible bedroom windows
bar parking lot and Halloween street coverage
hospital room and sanatorium flashback spaces

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond simple inserts and possible cleanup.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, broken glass, hair-cutting makeup continuity, weapon props, and a few fight beats.

rights_flags.detail: Tom Cruise is referenced by name via the smiling mask worn by the stalker.
AC/DC is referenced on Ashley’s T-shirt.
George Bush is referenced in the Halloween TV report as a costume/impersonation.
Spock, Jason, Dorothy, and other copyrighted/pop-culture costume references appear in the Halloween sequence.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: limited theatrical or streamer original thriller with strong genre thumbnail appeal.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the spend contained, but the script needs multiple night exteriors, several house interiors, a campus footprint, police coverage, and repeated attack setups with continuity-heavy hair and makeup effects.

casting.note: The lead is a large female ensemble with distinct types, and the Janice/Samantha reveal depends on an actress who can play authority, buried damage, and late-story menace in one package.

development.note: The final Janice/Samantha reveal reframes the entire mystery, so the script’s buy-in depends on the audience accepting a late identity shift after a long stretch of apparent procedural certainty.

comp_set.title: Scream
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like Scream, this is a youth-targeted slasher-thriller that uses a recognizable social group, self-aware banter, and a masked predator to drive suspense.

comp_set.title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
comp_set.why_it_comps: The shared-past guilt and revenge structure, plus the teen/young-adult ensemble under siege, puts it in the same commercial neighborhood.

comp_set.title: The Gift
comp_set.why_it_comps: The story’s buried-trauma reveal and small-town menace echo the way The Gift turns a community secret into a thriller engine.

comp_set.title: The Crush
comp_set.why_it_comps: The voyeuristic obsession, sexual threat, and domestic intrusion are aligned with the same stalker-thriller DNA.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre audiences who like female-ensemble thrillers with a revenge backstory and a nasty, voyeuristic threat engine.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 18-34 with a secondary 35+ horror/thriller audience; strongest with women and genre fans who respond to campus-set danger and serial-killer mystery.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary suburban and campus locations, modest stunt work, and practical effects keep this in indie feature territory despite the multiple attack sequences.

lane_fit.detail: The script sits in a lane where a sharp hook, a strong female ensemble, and a nasty villain reveal can sell the package without needing tentpole scale. It is most attractive to buyers who want a commercial genre title with a clear thumbnail and a contained production footprint.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the mystery resolves into a closed revenge backstory, and no supporting character is built as a separate franchise anchor.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a repeatable visual calling card that is easy to market and easy for audiences to remember after the credits. Buyers looking for a genre hook can sell the image in one sentence and one thumbnail.
strengths.evidence: Every attack repeats the same ritual: the intruder cuts the women’s hair, whispers 'you’re not so pretty now,' and leaves them marked.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble banter has real snap.
strengths.what_it_means: The girls feel like a social group rather than interchangeable victims, which makes the threat engine more engaging and gives the movie a broader teen/young-adult appeal. That kind of chemistry is what casting directors and directors look for when they want a thriller to feel alive between scares.
strengths.evidence: The party scenes, classroom exchanges, and poolside conversations all give Ashley, Megan, Sarah, and the others distinct voices and rhythms.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Janice reveal re-frames the whole story.
strengths.what_it_means: A late identity flip gives the script a second commercial engine: not just who is stalking them, but why the past is still bleeding into the present. That kind of reveal is attractive to buyers because it creates a clean trailer turn and a strong post-reveal conversation point.
strengths.evidence: The final unmasking of the attacker as Professor Janice Evans, followed by the Samantha flashback, changes the meaning of the entire investigation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The campus setting is instantly legible.
strengths.what_it_means: College bedrooms, parties, classrooms, and campus parking lots give the movie a familiar but marketable arena where voyeurism feels structurally plausible. That makes the script easy to position for genre buyers who want a contemporary, youth-facing thriller.
strengths.evidence: The attacks repeatedly happen in dorm-like bedrooms, at parties, and around the college grounds where the women live and study.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, sellable stalker-thriller with a memorable visual signature, a female ensemble that actually talks like a group of friends, and a late reveal that turns the mystery into a revenge story. It sits in a buyer-friendly indie lane: contemporary locations, practical effects, and a thumbnail-ready premise that can be packaged without tentpole spend.

items.area: The attack pattern repeats before the reveal lands.
items.detail: Several set pieces follow the same beat: voyeurism, intrusion, hair-cutting, escape. That gives the movie a clear signature, but it also means the middle section risks feeling procedural until the Janice turn changes the frame.

items.area: The final twist depends on a late identity shift.
items.detail: Janice’s Samantha reveal is the script’s biggest swing, but it arrives after a long stretch where the audience has been trained to track Wesley as the main threat. That makes the ending a development-sensitive sell, because the buyer has to believe the audience will accept the recontextualization rather than feel the floor move under them.

items.area: The hard-R assault material narrows the lane.
items.detail: The repeated sexual threat, forced restraint, and explicit predatory behavior push this into mature genre territory with a narrower buyer pool than a standard thriller. It is viable for streaming and specialty genre buyers, but it is not a broad theatrical play.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid, but the men are mostly functions.
items.detail: The girls have distinct voices, but most of the male characters — Dave, Wesley, the detectives, the father figures — are built as plot utilities or attitude carriers. That keeps the story moving, but it limits the relationship depth outside the central predator-victim dynamic.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is structural: it leans on a repeated attack pattern and then asks the audience to absorb a late identity reversal as the real engine of the story. Add the mature assault content, and this is a sharper niche buy than a broad commercial thriller.
